title: How Mars Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a morning-edition banter about Ash Wednesday, a NPR listener email, and a recent Alan Hills Martian meteorite (ALH84001) fossil claim. They then survey Mars: early fascination via Schiaparelli's canals and Percival Lowell's writings, the myth of the War of the Worlds radio panic, and NASA's Mars focus after the Shuttle program. The main segment covers how Mars formed and evolved (accretion, volcanism, atmosphere loss, the Great Desiccation), its surface features (Southern Highlands, northern plains, Tharsis, Elysium, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris), the polar caps and water ice found by Phoenix, perchlorate toxicity, and the interior compared with Earth's (core, mantle, lack of plate tectonics). Further discussion covers the thin CO2 atmosphere, terraforming, seasons and dust storms, the search for water and life (methane findings, Greenland bacteria, contamination risks), the Face on Mars photo, Mars in pop culture, and a listener email on food cravings and processed food engineering.
topics: War of the Worlds radio broadcast panic

segments.title: Opening banter and Martian meteorite news
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Ash Wednesday coincidences, a listener email from NPR, and new claims that the Alan Hills Martian meteorite shows fossilized nanobacteria.

segments.title: Early fascination with Mars
segments.summary: Schiaparelli's canal map and Lowell's civilization claims shaped popular ideas of Mars; the War of the Worlds panic is described as largely a newspaper-driven myth; NASA's post-Shuttle Mars focus and budget hearing are mentioned.
topics: War of the Worlds panic myth

segments.title: How Mars formed
segments.summary: Mars formed by accretion like Earth, was struck by meteors, had volcanism and a period of water and rain, then cooled and lost its atmosphere. Its smaller size is cited as the reason it cooled faster.

segments.title: Olympus Mons and Mars volcanoes
segments.summary: Volcanic activity thickened the atmosphere and the volcanoes went dormant about three billion years ago, cutting off heat and gas. Olympus Mons is compared with Mauna Loa and Everest.

segments.title: Mars surface regions and canyons
segments.summary: The surface is divided into Southern Highlands, northern plains and polar regions; Tharsis and Elysium are crustal upwarps; Valles Marineris is a canyon system larger than the Grand Canyon.

segments.title: Polar caps, water ice, and perchlorate
segments.summary: Polar caps have CO2 dry ice over water ice; Phoenix found water in soil and perchlorate, a toxic compound that poses a challenge for human missions. Elon Musk's Mars ambitions are mentioned.

segments.title: Mars interior compared with Earth
segments.summary: Mars's core is smaller and probably iron with sulfur, possibly not molten, which explains its weak magnetic field. Mars lacks moving plates, so it has no active volcanoes or earthquakes like Earth's fault lines. Mars's surface is rusty due to iron oxide.

segments.title: Mars atmosphere, seasons, and dust storms
segments.summary: Mars has a thin CO2 atmosphere, large daily temperature swings, a day about 40 minutes longer than Earth's, and a year nearly twice as long. Spring dust storms can envelop the planet for months. Terraforming is proposed as a long-term idea.

segments.title: Water, methane, and the search for life
segments.summary: Water is essential to life, NASA's follow-the-water strategy is described, methane findings were revised downward, and extremophile bacteria and contamination risks are discussed. The Face on Mars and Mars in pop culture close the segment.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give website and social media contact information.
